In each `CLUSTER NODES` line you see the address `ip:port@busport`, the role, the master it replicates, a connection state, and for primaries the slots owned. The second port, `16379`, is the **cluster bus** (data port plus 10000) over which nodes gossip; it must be reachable between nodes, which in real firewalls is an often-forgotten rule.

#### Step 2: which slot is my key in?

The slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384`. You can ask any node:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec c-node1 redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:1001
(integer) 181
$ docker exec c-node1 redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT stock:sku-1001
(integer) 6106
$ docker exec c-node1 redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT cart:u-17
(integer) 14402
blocks.title: Slots of ShopStream keys

blocks.text:
Slot 181 lives on the first primary (0 to 5460), 6106 on the second, 14402 on the third. So these three keys land on three different machines.

#### Step 3: get redirected

Connect to node 1 **without** cluster mode and write a key that belongs elsewhere:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec -it c-node1 redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> SET stock:sku-1001 50
(error) MOVED 6106 172.30.0.12:6379
127.0.0.1:6379> SET product:1001:name "Steel Mug"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> EXIT
blocks.title: A plain client meets MOVED

blocks.text: `MOVED 6106 172.30.0.12:6379` means: "slot 6106 is not mine; ask 172.30.0.12". The server never forwards the request for you. A cluster-aware client keeps a map of slots to nodes, learns it at startup, sends each command straight to the right node, and updates the map when it receives `MOVED`. `redis-cli -c` does the following for you:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec -it c-node1 redis-cli -c
127.0.0.1:6379> SET stock:sku-1001 50
-> Redirected to slot [6106] located at 172.30.0.12:6379
OK
172.30.0.12:6379> GET stock:sku-1001
"50"
172.30.0.12:6379> GET cart:u-17
-> Redirected to slot [14402] located at 172.30.0.13:6379
(nil)
172.30.0.13:6379> EXIT
blocks.title: Cluster mode follows redirects

blocks.text:
Notice the prompt changing to show which node you are talking to. Spring Data Redis and Lettuce do the same thing programmatically with a topology refresh; the Java chapters show how to configure it.

#### Step 4: multi-key commands and hash tags

A command touching several keys works only if all the keys are in the same slot. Otherwise:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec -it c-node1 redis-cli -c
127.0.0.1:6379> MSET cart:u-17 x stock:sku-1001 49
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot
blocks.title: CROSSSLOT

blocks.text: A **hash tag** fixes this: if a key contains `{...}`, only the text between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed. Put the entity id in braces and everything about that entity lands in one slot:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {cart:u-17}:items
(integer) 14402
127.0.0.1:6379> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {cart:u-17}:meta
(integer) 14402
127.0.0.1:6379> MSET {cart:u-17}:items 3 {cart:u-17}:meta "updated"
-> Redirected to slot [14402] located at 172.30.0.13:6379
OK
172.30.0.13:6379> EXIT
blocks.title: Hash tags force co-location

blocks.text:
Both keys hash exactly like the string `cart:u-17` (same slot 14402 as the plain key above), so a `MULTI/EXEC` transaction or a Lua script over them is allowed. The price is that all of one customer's data lives on one node, so one very hot tag is a hot shard. Choose tags to group things that are used together, not "everything of a tenant".

#### Step 5: kill a primary

Write some data, then stop the node that owns slots 0 to 5460 and watch the cluster heal.

blocks.code:
$ docker stop c-node1
c-node1
$ sleep 10
$ docker exec c-node2 redis-cli CLUSTER NODES | grep -E "172.30.0.1[15]"
de0cf6ef... 172.30.0.15:6379@16379 master - 0 1760086620000 7 connected 0-5460
017211931... 172.30.0.11:6379@16379 master,fail - 1760086608000 1760086606000 1 disconnected
$ docker exec c-node2 redis-cli CLUSTER INFO | head -n 1
cluster_state:ok
blocks.title: Failover

blocks.text: The replica on `172.30.0.15` noticed (through the other primaries voting) that its primary had been unreachable for longer than the node timeout and was promoted; it now owns slots 0 to 5460 and the cluster state is `ok` again. The old primary is shown as `master,fail`. Bring it back:

blocks.code:
$ docker start c-node1
c-node1
$ sleep 5
$ docker exec c-node2 redis-cli CLUSTER NODES | grep 172.30.0.11
017211931... 172.30.0.11:6379@16379 slave de0cf6ef... 0 1760086640000 7 connected
$ docker exec c-node1 redis-cli --cluster check 172.30.0.11:6379 | tail -n 3
[OK] All nodes agree about slots configuration.
>>> Check for open slots...
>>> Check slots coverage...
blocks.title: The old primary returns as a replica

blocks.text:
It rejoined by itself, learned from gossip that it had lost its slots, and became a replica of its former replica. No operator command was needed.

**Try it.** Stop **both** a primary and its replica (`c-node2` and `c-node6`) and run `CLUSTER INFO` on another node: with the default `cluster-require-full-coverage yes` the state becomes `fail` and the whole cluster stops answering queries, because slots 5461 to 10922 have no owner. That default is a deliberate consistency choice, and the cluster chapters explain when to relax it.

**What to observe.** Three ranges of slots; `MOVED` and `-c`; `CROSSSLOT` and hash tags; the bus port; automatic promotion; the old primary returning as a replica.

**Cleanup.**

blocks.code: $ docker compose down -v
blocks.title: Terminal
Gotcha
blocks.text: Reach the cluster from inside the network, or announce reachable addresses. The nodes tell clients to connect to `172.30.0.x`, an address that exists only inside the Docker network. From your laptop `redis-cli -c -p ...` against a published port will be redirected to unreachable IPs and hang. Run clients as containers on `shopnet`, as in this lab, or configure `cluster-announce-ip` and port mappings consciously. The same issue appears whenever a cluster sits behind NAT or a load balancer.

### LAB 2.9 · Lab: Benchmarking and the pipelining effect

**Goal.** Measure throughput and latency with `redis-benchmark`, then see what pipelining, payload size, client count and fsync policy do to them. About 25 minutes.

The numbers below are **illustrative** (a laptop-class machine, Redis and the benchmark on the same host through the loopback interface). Yours will differ a lot; what you should compare are the ratios. Benchmarks that run on the same machine as the server are good for relative comparisons and bad as capacity figures.

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name bench -p 6390:6379 redis:8
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -q -n 100000 -c 50 -t set,get
SET: 118343.20 requests per second, p50=0.239 msec
GET: 136612.02 requests per second, p50=0.207 msec
blocks.title: Start a clean server to measure

blocks.text: `-n` is the total number of requests, `-c` the number of parallel client connections (default 50), `-t` selects which tests to run, and `-q` prints one summary line per test. `p50` is the median latency. Redis commands are small; the cost per request is dominated by the network round trip, not by Redis. Now batch 16 commands per round trip with `-P 16`:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -q -n 200000 -c 50 -t set,get -P 16
SET: 574712.69 requests per second, p50=0.863 msec
GET: 1190476.25 requests per second, p50=0.495 msec
blocks.title: Pipelining

blocks.text:
Throughput rose four to nine times. Latency per **batch** went up (each reply now waits for 16 commands), but the cost per command fell, because the client no longer pays a network round trip for each one and the server does fewer system calls. This is the effect the pipelining chapter explains with numbers, and the reason the Java clients let you batch commands.

#### Vary one thing at a time

blocks.code:
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -q -n 100000 -t set -d 4096
SET: 98039.22 requests per second, p50=0.263 msec
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -q -n 100000 -t set -r 1000000
SET: 117647.06 requests per second, p50=0.247 msec
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -q -n 100000 LPUSH queue:test __rand_int__
LPUSH: 124223.60 requests per second, p50=0.231 msec
$ docker exec bench redis-cli DBSIZE
(integer) 95388
blocks.title: Payload size, random keys and a custom command

blocks.text:
`-d 4096` uses 4 KB values instead of the default 3 bytes (larger payloads cost more bandwidth and copying). `-r` `1000000` makes each request use a random key among a million; without `-r` every request hits the same key, which flatters caching in the CPU. The last benchmark runs any command you give it and replaces `__rand_int__` with a random number. Look at `DBSIZE` afterwards: the benchmark **wrote tens of thousands of keys** into your server (100000 requests spread over a million possible keys). Never run `redis-benchmark` against a server whose data you care about.

#### The full latency picture

Without `-q` you get the whole report:

blocks.code:
$ docker exec bench redis-benchmark -n 100000 -t get -c 50
====== GET ======
  100000 requests completed in 0.78 seconds
  50 parallel clients
  3 bytes payload
  keep alive: 1
  multi-thread: no

Latency by percentile distribution:
0.000% <= 0.087 milliseconds (cumulative count 1)
50.000% <= 0.207 milliseconds (cumulative count 51004)
99.219% <= 0.431 milliseconds (cumulative count 99250)
100.000% <= 2.847 milliseconds (cumulative count 100000)

Summary:
  throughput summary: 128205.13 requests per second
  latency summary (msec):
          avg       min       p50       p95       p99       max
        0.208     0.040     0.207     0.287     0.399     2.847
blocks.title: Full report (abridged)

blocks.text:
Averages hide the tail. For SLAs people watch p95, p99 and the maximum, because a user who hits the slow 1 percent notices. The occasional multi-millisecond maximum is typical of a shared machine.

#### What durability costs

Start a second server that fsyncs the AOF on every write and compare:

blocks.code:
$ docker run -d --name bench-always -p 6391:6379 redis:8 \
    redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync always
$ docker run -d --name bench-sec -p 6392:6379 redis:8 \
    redis-server --appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec
$ docker exec bench-always redis-benchmark -q -n 20000 -t set
SET: 9876.54 requests per second, p50=4.911 msec
$ docker exec bench-sec redis-benchmark -q -n 100000 -t set
SET: 105263.16 requests per second, p50=0.263 msec
blocks.title: appendfsync always versus everysec

blocks.text:
The ratio is the point (illustrative figures): with `always`, every write waits for the disk, so throughput is limited by your storage's `fsync` latency; `everysec` runs near memory speed and accepts up to about a second of loss. Run it on a cloud disk and on a laptop SSD and you will see very different `always` numbers, which is why persistence settings should be benchmarked on production-like hardware. Pipelining softens the cost of `always` considerably, because many commands share one `fsync` (try `-P 16`).

#### Reading benchmarks honestly

- The load generator is a program too. With a fast server you can saturate the **benchmark's** CPU first; use `--threads` `4` (available in current versions) or run it on a separate machine.
- Default tests use tiny values and one key shape. Your workload has bigger values, mixed commands and Lua scripts. Benchmark your own mix, with your client library, from where your application runs.
- Containers, virtual networks and noisy neighbours change latency. Compare like with like and repeat runs.
- `redis-benchmark` shows peak behaviour, not the effect of persistence rewrites, replication or eviction; run it while those are active if they matter.
- For richer workloads the Redis project maintains `memtier_benchmark`, which supports ratios of reads to writes and key distributions.

**What to observe.** Pipelining multiplies throughput; payload size and key randomness change results; the tail latency tells more than the average; `fsync` policy dominates write speed.

**Cleanup.**

blocks.code: $ docker rm -f bench bench-always bench-sec
blocks.title: Terminal
Real world
blocks.text: Benchmark numbers you publish internally should always state: hardware, Redis version and config, client count, pipeline depth, payload size, key space, and whether the client ran on the same machine. Without those, nobody can reproduce or compare them, and a number like "Redis does a million operations per second" travels without its context and misleads the next team.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The labs give you muscle memory: `SET`/`INCR`/`EXPIRE`, lists and sets, hashes and sorted sets, streams with groups, persistence modes, replication, Sentinel and Cluster.
- Persistence is a trade between speed and the data-loss window: RDB loses since the last snapshot, AOF `everysec` about a second, AOF `always` almost nothing at a throughput cost.
- Asynchronous replication does not guarantee that acknowledged writes survive a failover; `WAIT` and `min-replicas-to-write` narrow the risk.
- Sentinel automates failover for one dataset; Cluster shards the keyspace into 16384 slots and needs a cluster-aware client, hash tags for multi-key operations, and reachable node addresses.
- Benchmark relative changes (pipelining, payload, fsync) on realistic hardware, and never against data you care about.
